summary: The babies and swaps of a shelamim, and their babies forever, are just like a shelamim. Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis argue whether the baby of a shelamim may be brought as a korban, and Rabbi Pappeyas tells how his family did bring one.

chunks.he: אֵלּוּ קָדָשִׁים שֶׁוַּלְדוֹתֵיהֶן וּתְמוּרוֹתֵיהֶן כַּיּוֹצֵא בָהֶן.
chunks.en: These are the korbanos whose babies and swaps are like them:
chunks.st: These are the sacrificial animals for which the halakhic status of their offspring and substitutes is like their own halakhic status:

chunks.en: The baby of a shelamim,
chunks.st: The offspring of peace offerings,

words.note: A korban that is shared: some is burned, some eaten by the Kohanim and some by the owners.

chunks.en: and their swaps, and their babies,
chunks.st: and their substitute animals,

chunks.en: and their babies' babies, until the end of the world,
chunks.st: and even the offspring of their offspring or their substitute animals, and even the offspring of their offspring, until the end of all time [ad sof kol ha’olam].

chunks.en: they are like a shelamim.
chunks.st: They are all endowed with the sanctity and halakhic status of peace offerings,

chunks.he: וּטְעוּנִים סְמִיכָה וּנְסָכִים וּתְנוּפָה וְחָזֶה וָשׁוֹק.
chunks.en: They need semichah, nesachim, waving, and the chest and thigh.
chunks.explain: The chest and thigh are waved and given to the Kohen.
chunks.st: and therefore they require placing hands on the head of the animal, and libations, and the waving of the breast and the thigh in order to give them to the priest.
chunks.stMore: Although the previous mishna stated plainly that the offspring of a peace offering is itself sacrificed as a peace offering, its status is actually subject to a dispute between the tanna’im.

words.note: Leaning hands on the animal's head.

summary: If someone set aside a female animal for an olah or an asham, which must be males, it grazes until it gets a blemish and is sold, and the money buys the right korban. The swap of an asham, and an asham whose owner died, are also sold, and the Rabbis argue what to do with the money.

chunks.en: If someone sets aside a female for an olah and it gives birth to a male,
chunks.st: In the case of one who designates a female animal as a burnt offering, which may be brought only from males, and that female gave birth to a male, although it is a male,

chunks.en: the baby grazes until it gets a blemish and is sold,
chunks.st: it is left to graze until it becomes unfit [sheyista’ev] and then it is sold,

chunks.en: and with its money he brings an olah.
chunks.st: and he brings a burnt offering with the money received for its sale.

chunks.en: It may be sold even without a blemish.
chunks.st: Therefore, it may be sold without a blemish, and a guilt offering is purchased with the money received for its sale.

summary: What is the difference between Rabbi Elazar and the Sages, if a gift korban is also an olah? Rabbi Elazar means the owner's own olah: he leans his hands on it and pays for its nesachim. A gift korban belongs to the whole community.

chunks.en: But isn't a gift korban also an olah?
chunks.st: But even according to the Rabbis, isn’t a gift offering also a burnt offering?

chunks.en: So what is the difference between the words of Rabbi
chunks.st: And what then is the difference between the statement of

chunks.en: Elazar and the words of the Sages?
chunks.st: Rabbi Elazar and the statement of the Rabbis?

chunks.en: Rather, when it comes as a person's own olah,
chunks.st: Rather,
chunks.stMore: the Rabbis are referring to a communal burnt offering and Rabbi Elazar is referring to an individual burnt offering, and there are several differences between these two offerings:

chunks.he: הוּא סוֹמֵךְ עָלֶיהָ וּמֵבִיא עָלֶיהָ נְסָכִין,
chunks.en: he leans his hands on it and brings nesachim with it,
chunks.st: When the animal comes as an individual burnt offering, the owner places his hands upon it and brings the accompanying meal offering and libations,

chunks.en: and its nesachim are paid by him.
chunks.st: and its libations come from his own property.

chunks.en: And if he was a Kohen,
chunks.st: If the owner of the animal was a priest,

chunks.en: he does its avodah and gets its hide.
chunks.st: the right to perform its Temple service and the right to its hide are his.

words.note: The service of bringing the korban.

chunks.en: But when it comes as a gift korban,
chunks.st: And when it is a communal gift offering, the owner of the animal that was sold

chunks.en: he does not lean his hands on it, and does not
chunks.st: does not place his hands upon it, as there is no placing of hands for communal offerings,

chunks.en: bring nesachim with it,
chunks.st: and he does not bring its libations; rather,

chunks.en: and its nesachim are paid by the community.
chunks.st: its libations are brought from the property of the community.

chunks.en: Even if he is a Kohen,
chunks.st: Furthermore, although the owner of the animal that was sold is a priest,

chunks.en: its avodah and its hide belong to the Kohanim on duty that week.
chunks.st: the right to perform its Temple service and the right to its hide are divided among the members of the priestly watch serving in the Temple that week.

words.note: The group of Kohanim serving in the Beis HaMikdash that week.

summary: The swaps of a bechor and maaser, and their babies, are like a bechor and maaser and are eaten once they get a blemish. The mishnah lists ways a bechor and maaser are different from all other korbanos.

chunks.en: The swap of a bechor and of maaser,
chunks.st: With regard to the substitute of a firstborn offering and the substitute of an animal tithe offering,

chunks.he: וּוְלָדָן, וּוְלַד וְלָדָן עַד סוֹף הָעוֹלָם,
chunks.en: and their babies and their babies' babies until the end of the world,
chunks.st: and the offspring of those substitutes and the offspring of their offspring until the end of time,

chunks.en: are like a bechor and like maaser,
chunks.st: the halakhic status of these animals is like that of a firstborn offering and like that of an animal tithe offering in that they must be treated with sanctity: They graze until they become blemished,

chunks.en: and are eaten by the owners once they have a blemish.
chunks.st: and at that point they may be eaten in their blemished state, the substitute of the firstborn by the priests and the substitute of the animal tithe by their owners.
chunks.stMore: They are not sacrificed upon the altar like the original firstborn and animal tithe offerings.

chunks.en: What is the difference between a bechor and maaser
chunks.st: What is the practical difference between a firstborn offering and an animal tithe offering

chunks.en: and all other korbanos?
chunks.st: and all the other sacrificial animals?

chunks.en: All other korbanos are sold in the butcher shop,
chunks.st: The difference is that all the other sacrificial animals that were blemished and redeemed are sold in the butchers’ market [ba’itliz],

chunks.en: and shechted in the butcher shop, and weighed by the pound,
chunks.st: and slaughtered in the butchers’ market, and weighed and sold by the litra, in the manner that non-sacred meat is slaughtered and sold. This is the case with regard to all consecrated animals

words.note: A unit of weight, like a pound.

chunks.en: except for a bechor and maaser.
chunks.st: except for the firstborn and animal tithe offerings, which are sold only from the home and not by the litra.

chunks.en: Other korbanos can be redeemed,
chunks.st: And in addition, all sacrificial animals that became blemished are subject to redemption through sale, at which point the money becomes sacred and the animal becomes non-sacred,

words.note: Buying it back so it becomes plain, and the money becomes holy.

chunks.en: and their swaps can be redeemed,
chunks.st: and their substitutes are also subject to redemption through sale.

chunks.en: except for a bechor and maaser.
chunks.st: This is true for all consecrated animals, except for the firstborn and animal tithe offerings, which are not subject to redemption.

chunks.en: And korbanos may come from outside Eretz Yisrael,
chunks.st: And all sacrificial animals come to be sacrificed in the Temple even from outside of Eretz Yisrael,

chunks.en: except for a bechor and maaser.
chunks.st: except for the firstborn and animal tithe offerings, which should not be brought from outside Eretz Yisrael ab initio.

chunks.en: If they came without blemishes,
chunks.st: But if they came unblemished,

chunks.en: they are brought as korbanos. And if they have blemishes,
chunks.st: they are sacrificed in the Temple like a regular firstborn or animal tithe offering coming from Eretz Yisrael; and if they are blemished animals,

chunks.en: they are eaten by the owners with their blemish.
chunks.st: they may be eaten in their blemished state, the firstborns by the priests and the animal tithes by their owners.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon said:
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: What is the reason?
chunks.st: What is the reason for this last difference between them? It is

chunks.he: שֶׁהַבְּכוֹר וְהַמַּעֲשֵׂר יֵשׁ לָהֶן פַּרְנָסָה בִמְקוֹמָן,
chunks.en: A bechor and maaser can be taken care of where they are,
chunks.st: that the firstborn and animal tithe offerings have a remedy in their place outside Eretz Yisrael, as they can graze until they become blemished and then can be eaten there.
chunks.stMore: It is not necessary to bring them to Eretz Yisrael in order to eat them.

chunks.en: but all other korbanos, even
chunks.st: But with regard to all other sacrificial animals, even

chunks.en: if they got a blemish,
chunks.st: if a blemish develops in them,

chunks.en: they stay holy.
chunks.st: these animals remain in their sanctity, and one must redeem them and bring another offering with the money of their redemption. Therefore, when they are unblemished it is proper to bring these animals themselves to Eretz Yisrael.
